wine.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Kellerberg
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Kellerberg above Dürnstein: steep dry stone terraces of Gföhl gneiss facing south to south east, sheltered from the westerly winds of the Ice Ages, so patches of loess survive. Its name, from the baroque Kellerschlössl of Dürnstein, dates only from 1787 and gathered several smaller vineyards.
wine.making: Picked by hand late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires of every wine and the ripeness of a Smaragd asks. The codex of the Vinea Wachau forbids any enrichment of the must and allows a Smaragd no hint of oak, and the wine is fermented dry; the house speaks of as little intervention as it can manage in the cellar.
wine.glass: Mango, passion fruit and pineapple over ripe yellow peach and wet stone; dense and broad for a dry Riesling, with high extract, ripe acidity and an alcohol that reads as weight rather than heat, and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous on release, it is at its fullest after eight to ten years, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems closed; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named for the emerald lizard.
The single vineyard; Austrian law asks for the word Ried before a vineyard's name.
The older form on the label, the Kellerberg of Dürnstein, before Ried was required.
The appellation since the 2020 vintage; its single vineyard wines are Grüner Veltliner or Riesling alone.

records.table: F.X. Pichler's Riesling Smaragd Ried Kellerberg grows on steep gneiss terraces above Dürnstein in the Wachau. Dry yet broad, with mango and ripe peach over stone, it carries the weight of the valley's ripest style, so pour it cool rather than cold.
records.story: In the middle of the nineteenth century, as the house tells it, a forebear of the family, a grower from Rohrendorf near Krems, moved into the Wachau, and a grandson bought a property at Oberloiben in 1898; the house dates its winery there to 1905. The F.X. of the name, a later grower of the family who studied at the wine school of Krems and worked vintages in Germany and Alsace, set out to show each site at the full ripeness of its grapes. In 1983 the growers of the valley founded the Vinea Wachau, with its codex against enrichment and its three styles of Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, and F.X. Pichler stood with it from the beginning. Two years later a scandal over doctored sweet wines emptied Austria's export markets and brought a strict new wine law. The Riesling Kellerberg of 1990 was, by the house's own account, the wine that carried its name abroad, as the dry Smaragd wines of the Wachau led Austria's recovery. In 2009 the family moved into a new winery at Oberloiben, and since the 2020 vintage the Kellerberg has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC. To a sommelier the wine is the measure of how much ripeness a dry Riesling can carry.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Loibenberg
others.note: Warmer and broader, from the hill above Loiben, the direct comparison with the Kellerberg.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Kellerberg
others.note: Grüner Veltliner at full Smaragd weight from the same terraces.

others.name: Unendlich
others.note: A selection made only in years the house judges fit, a Riesling from 1998 and a Grüner Veltliner from 2003; the name means endless.

traps: F.X. Pichler is not Rudi Pichler or Pichler-Krutzler: several unrelated Pichler estates work the Wachau, so read the initials.
Smaragd is a trademark of the Vinea Wachau, a growers' association, not a rank in Austrian law; it names ripeness, not the vineyard.
A Smaragd is dry: the word promises ripeness and weight, never sweetness.

cards.front: F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg: what rock lies under its terraces?
cards.back: Gföhl gneiss, a metamorphic rock, with patches of loess that the Ice Ages left on the sheltered south east slope.

cards.front: What does the word Smaragd on F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg label promise, and whose rule is it?
cards.back: A dry wine of at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol with no hint of oak, under the Vinea Wachau's own codex.

questions.q: A guest reads Smaragd on F.X. Pichler's Riesling Ried Kellerberg and expects a sweet wine. What do you tell them?
opts: It is dry: the word marks the Wachau's ripest dry style
It is late picked and keeps some natural sugar
It is a sweet wine of grapes touched by noble rot
It is a dry wine aged a year in new oak
questions.exp: Smaragd is the Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, fermented dry to at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol; the codex allows it no hint of oak, so the new oak answer is wrong as well.

questions.q: By the house's own account, the Riesling Kellerberg of which vintage first carried the name of F.X. Pichler abroad?
questions.exp: The house dates its breakthrough abroad to the Kellerberg of 1990; 1983 is the founding of the Vinea Wachau, 1985 Austria's wine scandal and 2009 the house's new winery.

wine.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Singerriedel at Spitz, first recorded in 1486, narrow terraces held by dry stone walls: shallow, sandy, meagre soil over paragneiss, with mica schist and bands of quartzite lower down; Riesling grows on the steep terraces and Grüner Veltliner at the foot.
wine.making: Picked by hand on the terraces late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires and the ripeness of a Smaragd asks, with no enrichment under the Vinea Wachau's codex. The wine is fermented dry in stainless steel and is often then raised in large wooden casks of three to five thousand litres, which give it no taste of oak; some vintages stay in steel.
wine.glass: Ripe yellow peach, apricot and lime zest over wet stone and a smoky note of the rock, with orange blossom; full and creamy yet dry, with firm acidity and a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it settles after five years or so, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more, gaining honey and dried apricot.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems tight; a large white wine glass.

records.table: Franz Hirtzberger's Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel grows on narrow dry stone terraces at Spitz, in the western Wachau. Ripe peach and apricot over stone, full and creamy yet dry, it is a Riesling that rewards a decade in the cellar.
records.story: The Hirtzbergers are a family of growers at Spitz, in the western Wachau. The modern estate begins with the grower of the house who took over his parents' holding in 1948: by the account of the Vinea Wachau, he bottled its wine for the first time and picked out the terraces of single vineyards the family farms. In 1983 he was one of the growers who founded the Vinea Wachau, the association whose codex forbids enrichment and whose Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd measure the ripeness of a dry wine. His son took over the estate that same year, saw it through the wine scandal of 1985 and the strict law that followed, and led the association from 1988 to 2012, as the dry wines of the Wachau found their way abroad. The Singerriedel, the steep wall of narrow terraces on paragneiss at Spitz, gave the house its signature Riesling, picked late for Smaragd and fermented dry. Since the 2020 vintage the vineyard has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC. In 2014 a son of the family founded a separate estate, the Weinhofmeisterei at Wösendorf, so a sommelier reads the whole name on the label: the Singerriedel of Spitz is Franz Hirtzberger's.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Hochrain

Honivogl and Singerriedel are vineyard names, not producers.
Smaragd names the Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, never a sweet wine.

report: Founded is left empty: one account has the family buying its first vines at Spitz in the late nineteenth century and another speaks of a farm of the thirteenth century; no house page was found to settle it.

The grower of 1948 (born 1923, died 2007, by the Vinea Wachau's own notice) is described rather than named, as his dates rest on that one source; his son and grandson are living and are not named, and the brother who founded the Weinhofmeisterei in 2014 should be added to people.json by the read together agent (Mathias Hirtzberger).

The grower of 1948 as a founder of the Vinea Wachau in 1983 rests on the association's own notice and its fortieth anniversary release, which lists him among the founding fathers (the Sommelier Academy agrees); his first bottling is on the house's profile there, with no year given; the son's leadership from 1988 to 2012 rests on the Vinea Wachau's own notice, with Decanter calling him its long standing president.

The making rests on Falstaff's entries for several vintages (steel tank and large wooden barrel) and a merchant's listing that gives casks of three to five thousand litres; Falstaff lists steel alone for one vintage, so the record says most vintages.
The Ried Hochrain Riesling Smaragd is attested by Falstaff and a second listing only as a wine, so its note says nothing of the site.
The table and the ageing keep the library's view of a ripe, long lived Riesling; the region line's 'richest, most honeyed' is a judgement and is not repeated.

wine.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Schütt, astride the boundary of Dürnstein and Unterloiben, on a fan of stream debris at the mouth of the Menthalgraben, between the Höhereck and the Loibenberg: deep, sandy and stony soil of weathered gneiss, poor in fine earth, so it drains fast.
wine.making: Picked by hand late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires, with no enrichment under the Vinea Wachau's codex. The wine is fermented dry and raised mostly in large, old oak casks, with some stainless steel beside them; the casks are big and old, so they give the wine air and texture rather than a taste of wood.
wine.glass: White pepper, green pear and quince over lentils and wet stone, with tobacco leaf as it ages; dense and savoury rather than fruity, dry and long, with a fine, stony grip.
wine.ageing: Dense and savoury young, it gains depth over five to ten years, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named for the emerald lizard.

records.table: Emmerich Knoll's Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt comes from a stony fan of gneiss at Unterloiben and wears the baroque Saint Urban label. Peppery, savoury and dense, it is long lived, so give it years in the cellar and some air in the glass.
records.story: The Knolls have grown vines at Unterloiben, at the eastern end of the Wachau, since the early nineteenth century. By the house's account Knoll wine went into glass bottles from the 1950s, and in 1962 the baroque image of Saint Urban first appeared on the label, where it has stayed. In 1983 the growers of the valley founded the Vinea Wachau, whose codex forbids enrichment and whose Smaragd marks the ripest dry wine, and the Knoll wines carry its styles. After the wine scandal of 1985 and the strict law that followed it, the house kept its own pace, with late picking and large old oak casks. From 1988 it added a Vinothekfüllung, a dry selection of late picked Grüner Veltliner made in nearly every year, joined by a Riesling in 2000. Its vineyards lie around the village, the Loibenberg, the Kellerberg and the Kreutles among them, with the Pfaffenberg across the border in the Kremstal, yet the house names the Schütt before them all. Since the 2020 vintage the Schütt has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC. To a sommelier it is the proof that Grüner Veltliner from the Wachau can last for decades.

wine.name: Riesling Zöbinger Heiligenstein Alte Reben
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the Kamptal DAC; Erste Lage, marked 1ÖTW, of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from old vines, a few of them planted before the Second World War.
wine.sites: The Zöbinger Heiligenstein above Zöbing, a bare hill of Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic grains, its face held by dry stone terraces built by hand from the 1920s; part of the house's share is trained on the Lyra, a divided, lyre shaped trellis.
wine.making: The juice ferments in stainless steel at fifteen to twenty degrees Celsius, and the wine then rests on its lees, in steel and in large wooden casks, until it is bottled some months later.
wine.glass: Yellow peach, apricot and orange peel over smoke, warm stone and dried thyme; dry and firm, with fine, salty acidity, a silky weight and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it opens after five to seven years, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard on the sandstone hill above Zöbing; newer labels print Ried Heiligenstein.
Old vines: the house's old plantings on the Heiligenstein.
The Traditionsweingüter's own mark for a site it ranks Erste Lage; Austrian law framed classified sites only in 2023.
The appellation since the 2008 vintage, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling above all.

records.table: Bründlmayer's Riesling Alte Reben comes from old vines on the Zöbinger Heiligenstein, the Kamptal's hill of desert sandstone above Zöbing. It is dry and firm, apricot and orange peel over smoke and warm stone, and it keeps for decades.
records.story: Bründlmayer is a family estate of Langenlois, in the Kamptal, whose Heuriger stands in a Renaissance vintner's house in the town. Its signature hill, the Heiligenstein above Zöbing, is usually said to appear in a monastic register of 1280 as Hellenstein, for the heat of its bare slope, before the name became Heiligenstein, the holy stone. From the 1920s dry stone terraces were built by hand on its face, and some of the vines on it lived through the Second World War. In 1980 the son of the house took over from his parents; in time part of the hill was trained on the Lyra trellis, and a sparkling wine made in the bottle joined the range. In 1996 the Bründlmayers helped a new family to take over the running of Schloss Gobelsburg nearby. The Kamptal DAC followed with the 2008 vintage, and from 2010 the Traditionsweingüter, a private association of estates, ranked its members' sites, the Heiligenstein among its Erste Lagen. In 2015 the vineyards were certified organic. Alte Reben is the house's selection from its old vines on the hill: to a sommelier, Austrian Riesling grown on desert sandstone rather than on the Wachau's gneiss.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm
others.note: Grüner Veltliner from deep loess and loam on the south east side of the Heiligenstein, rich and long.

others.name: Riesling Ried Heiligenstein
others.note: The hill's Riesling without the old vine selection, the step below the Alte Reben.

others.name: Extra Brut Reserve
others.note: Sparkling wine made by the traditional method, its second fermentation in the bottle.

traps: The Heiligenstein is Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic grains, not limestone, whatever its holy stone name suggests.
The Kamptal is not the Wachau: Smaragd, Federspiel and Steinfeder never appear on Bründlmayer's labels.
1ÖTW is the private mark of the Traditionsweingüter, not a rank in Austrian wine law.

report: Founded is left empty: one lexicon dates the family's tradition to 1581, but the house's own pages read here gave no year, so the story does not use it.
The register of 1280 and the name Hellenstein rest on the wein.plus lexicon and a wine wiki, both read through search summaries, and are told as what is usually said.

The making rests on the house's own factsheets: steel at fifteen to twenty degrees and lees until bottling in the summer for 2018, steel then a wooden cask of 2,500 litres for 2023 (bottled in February 2024); the record says many vintages and the year after the harvest.

The terraces of the 1920s, the vines that lived through the war, fertiliser given up in 1979, the Lyra and the organic certificate of 2015 are the house's own account; the son who took over around 1980 is living and is not named.

wine.name: Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the Kamptal DAC; Erste Lage, marked 1ÖTW, of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter
wine.sites: The Lamm, on the south east side of the Heiligenstein, where the hill eases into gentler slopes: deep loess and loam, mixed with material washed down from the hill's Permian rock and volcanic stone.
wine.making: Fermented and matured in large traditional casks of five to six thousand litres, made of Austrian oak from the nearby Manhartsberg forest, with an occasional new cask among them. Under the Kamptal DAC a single vineyard wine may not be submitted for its state test number before April of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, quince and yellow apple over white pepper, lentils and toasted hazelnut, with a hint of honey; broad, creamy and dry, with fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to drink on release, it gains depth over five to ten years, and a strong vintage keeps for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard of loess and loam on the south east side of the Heiligenstein.
The Traditionsweingüter's own mark for a site it ranks Erste Lage; Austrian law framed classified sites only in 2023.
The appellation since the 2008 vintage, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling above all.

records.table: Schloss Gobelsburg's Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm grows in deep loess and loam on the south east side of the Heiligenstein, on an estate tied to the monks of Zwettl since 1171. Broad and dry, pear, quince and white pepper, it is matured in large Austrian oak casks.
records.story: In 1171, as the house tells it, the Cistercian monks of Zwettl Abbey received their first vineyards in the Kamptal, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg. The castle of Gobelsburg passed through many noble families until 1740, when its last aristocratic owner sold it to the abbey, which already held an estate at Kammern nearby; late in the eighteenth century, after a fire at Kammern, the making of the wine moved to Gobelsburg. The monks ran the cellar themselves until 1995. In 1996 a family took over the running of the estate on a long lease, with early help from the Bründlmayers of Langenlois, while the abbey kept the ownership. The new managers added a Tradition line, an ode to the cellar ways of Gobelsburg between 1800 and 1850. The Kamptal DAC came with the 2008 vintage, and the Traditionsweingüter, a private association of estates, ranked the Lamm and the Heiligenstein among its Erste Lagen. In 2021 the house marked eight hundred and fifty years of winegrowing. The Lamm is its fullest Grüner Veltliner: to a sommelier, a Kamptal wine of full weight from loess and loam, and a monastic estate's history in one glass.

questions.exp: The abbey bought the castle in 1740; its monks had held vineyards nearby since 1171, a family took over the running on a lease in 1996, and 2008 brought the Kamptal DAC.

report: Founded is the library's 1171, but by the house's own history 1171 is the year the monks of Zwettl received their first Kamptal vineyards, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg; the abbey bought the castle in 1740, so the plan's 'estate at Gobelsburg recorded from 1171' is loose.

The library's trap says the estate is run under lease by its winemaker; the house speaks of management by a family from 1996 with the abbey as owner, and no source read here gives a lease, so the record says the running of the estate.

The region's producers line has the Tradition wines made in old wooden casks moved on wheels, and the library has racking by the moon; neither was confirmed by any source read here, so the record says only an ode to the cellar ways of 1800 to 1850 (the house and Skurnik).
The casks of five thousand litres and more, a few new, rest on two importer notes for the 2019 and 2022 vintages; the Manhartsberg oak on the house's page and an importer.
The family that took over in 1996 and the couple of Bründlmayer who helped them are living and are not named.
The eight hundred and fiftieth year in 2021 rests on the house's jubilee edition and a wine travel page (Wine in Time).
